 Entertainment Every James Bond actor's age in his first 007 film, in chronological order 
 With the announcement of Robert Pattinson as the next 007 at 40 years old, let's look back at the James Bond actors' ages at their 007 debuts
 1 / 9 List slides Every James Bond actor's age in his first 007 film, in chronological order List slides Previous Start over By Colleen Cabili · Updated November 16, 2026 Add QZ to Google Illustration: Quartz
 The actors who launched James Bond on screen ranged in age from 29 to 45 at their debuts. That is a 16-year spread. Ian Fleming's novels place Bond in his mid-to-late thirties, and the novel Moonraker puts his age at 37. On film, the starting age has landed well above and well below that mark.
 The list below tracks James Bond actors' ages in chronological order, from Sean Connery in Dr. No in 1962 to Daniel Craig in Casino Royale in 2006. Each figure is the actor's age when his first Bond film reached theaters. None of them is an age at casting. Filming came before release, and the two numbers can differ. Connery, for example, was 31 while Dr. No was being shot and 32 when it opened.
 Six actors have played Bond in the official films produced by Eon Productions. They are Connery, George Lazenby, Roger Moore, Timothy Dalton, Pierce Brosnan and Craig. Their tenures varied widely. Lazenby made a single film. Dalton made two. Moore held the part for 12 years. Craig held it for 15, the longest continuous run of any Bond actor.
 Later films carried some actors well past Fleming's late-thirties Bond. Moore was 57 when A View to a Kill came out in 1985. Connery was 41 when he returned for Diamonds Are Forever in 1971, after Lazenby's one outing.
 The two extremes arrived within a few years of each other. Lazenby was 29 in On Her Majesty's Secret Service in 1969, the youngest debut. That made him three years younger than Connery at his start. Moore was 45 in Live and Let Die in 1973, the oldest debut. Of the six, Craig came nearest to the age Moonraker gives Bond. He was 38 in Casino Royale, one year older than the novel's figure.
 The seventh entry is Lashana Lynch, who plays Nomi in No Time to Die (2021). Her character holds the 007 number, though she does not play James Bond. She was 33 when the film was released.
 Each slide covers one performer, with birth year, age at debut and, where the record supports it, age in later films.
 Sean Connery was 32 when Dr. No made him the first James Bond 
 Illustration: Quartz
 Sean Connery was 32 when Dr. No reached theaters in 1962, making him the first actor to play James Bond in the official Eon Productions series. The Scottish actor was born in 1930.
 His screen career predated Bond by eight years. It began in 1954 with Lilacs in the Spring.
 The early films arrived in quick succession after Dr. No. From Russia With Love came out in 1963, when Connery was 33. Goldfinger followed in 1964, with Connery at 34. He was 35 for Thunderball in 1965 and 37 for You Only Live Twice in 1967.
 That pace put five Bond films in cinemas between 1962 and 1967, roughly one a year. Connery aged five years over the same stretch, going from 32 to 37.
 Connery then stepped away. George Lazenby took over the role for a single film, On Her Majesty's Secret Service, released in 1969. Connery came back for Diamonds Are Forever in 1971, when he was 41. That film was his last in the official series. Four years had passed since You Only Live Twice.
 In total, Connery played Bond in six Eon films over nine years, from 1962 to 1971. His age at each release rose from 32 to 41 across that run.
 His debut age makes him the second-youngest actor to debut as James Bond, according to ScreenRant . Only George Lazenby, who was 29 in On Her Majesty's Secret Service, began younger. ScreenRant also notes that some people mistakenly believe Connery was the youngest Bond.
 Roger Moore, Timothy Dalton, Pierce Brosnan and Daniel Craig were all older than 32 in their first Bond films. Craig came closest. He was still six years older at his Casino Royale debut than Connery was in Dr. No. Even at 41 in Diamonds Are Forever, Connery was four years younger than Moore was at his debut.
 George Lazenby was 29 in On Her Majesty's Secret Service, the youngest Bond 
 Illustration: Quartz
 George Lazenby was 29 when On Her Majesty's Secret Service reached theaters in 1969. He is the youngest actor to play James Bond in the official Eon Productions series. No actor since has debuted as 007 at a younger age.
 Lazenby was born in 1939, nine years after Sean Connery. He followed Connery into the part, taking over from the actor who had launched the film series with Dr. No in 1962.
 His tenure was the shortest of any Bond actor. On Her Majesty's Secret Service was the only Bond film Lazenby made.
 The film was also Lazenby's first movie role of any kind. He came to it from outside the acting world. He earned a living as a car salesman before moving into modeling. The work that first made his face known to the public was an advertisement for chocolate bars.
 He was an Australian model living in London when he landed the part. His acting experience amounted to little beyond television commercials. He is the only actor from Australia to have played Bond.
 Physical ability worked in his favor. Lazenby's athleticism impressed the people casting the film. During a fight audition, he reportedly broke a stuntman's nose.
 Lazenby has offered his own explanation for how he won the role. He credited his casting to his arrogance and his sure way with women.
 His youth record has held since 1969. Every actor who debuted as Bond after him was older at his first 007 film. Daniel Craig came closest, and he was still nine years older at his debut than Lazenby was at his.
 Roger Moore, Timothy Dalton and Pierce Brosnan were all in their 40s when their first Bond films opened. Dalton was 41 in The Living Daylights in 1987. Brosnan was 42 in GoldenEye in 1995. Moore was born in 1927, 12 years before Lazenby. His first Bond film arrived in 1973, four years after Lazenby's.
 Roger Moore was 45 in Live and Let Die, the oldest actor to debut as Bond 
 Illustration: Quartz
 Roger Moore was 45 when Live and Let Die opened in 1973. No actor has begun an official run as James Bond at an older age.
 Moore was born in 1927, three years before Sean Connery. He still followed the younger man into the role. Connery's last official Bond film, Diamonds Are Forever, had come out in 1971, two years before Moore's debut.
 Connery had been 32 when Dr. No opened in 1962. Moore's debut age was 13 years higher. Moore was also older in his first Bond film than Connery had been in his final official one.
 Moore made seven official Bond films, and his age climbed with each release. He was 46 in The Man With the Golden Gun (1974), which came out a year after his debut. He was 49 in The Spy Who Loved Me (1977). The three-year wait before that film was the longest gap between his Bond releases.
 He was 51 in Moonraker (1979). The Ian Fleming novel that shares the film's title gives Bond's age as 37. Moore was 14 years older than that on screen.
 From Moonraker on, his films arrived every two years. He was 53 in For Your Eyes Only (1981) and 55 in Octopussy (1983). His final outing, A View To A Kill, reached theaters in 1985, when he was 57.
 Moore's tenure ran 12 years, from Live and Let Die in 1973 to A View To A Kill in 1985. That was longer than Connery's official stretch, which covered six films over nine years. Daniel Craig later passed it with a 15-year run.
 None of the actors who followed matched Moore's starting age. Timothy Dalton was 41 when The Living Daylights opened in 1987. Pierce Brosnan was 42 in GoldenEye (1995), and Craig was 38 in Casino Royale (2006). Dalton, Moore's immediate successor, started four years younger than Moore had in 1973.
 Timothy Dalton was 41 when The Living Daylights opened in 1987 
 Illustration: Quartz
 Timothy Dalton was 41 when The Living Daylights opened in 1987, making him the fourth actor to play James Bond in the official Eon Productions series. Born in 1946, he made two films as 007.
 His second and last Bond film, Licence to Kill, reached theaters in 1989. Dalton was 43 by then. The two releases came two years apart. Only George Lazenby, with a single film, had a shorter tenure in the part.
 Dalton started as Bond at the same age Sean Connery had reached in his final official Bond film, Diamonds Are Forever. Dalton arrived at that age in the role 16 years after Connery's exit.
 Dalton's take on the character followed Roger Moore's and came before Pierce Brosnan's. Moore's last outing, A View to a Kill, was released two years before The Living Daylights. Dalton was also four years younger at his first Bond film than Moore had been at his. Moore debuted at 45 in Live and Let Die.
 Among the other debuts, Dalton sat near the top of the age range. He was 12 years older than Lazenby at his start and three years older than Daniel Craig would be in Casino Royale. Brosnan, his successor, was 42 when GoldenEye opened in 1995, one year older than Dalton at debut. That release came six years after Licence to Kill.
 Dalton was an established screen actor before taking the part. His film career began in 1968 with the role of Philip II in The Lion in Winter. That came 19 years before his first appearance as 007.
 He had also worked in spy thrillers before joining the series. In 1975 he played Charles Lord in Permission to Kill, 12 years ahead of The Living Daylights.
 Across his two films, Dalton's age on screen as Bond rose only from 41 to 43. That two-year spread is the narrowest of any actor who has made more than one official Bond film.
 Pierce Brosnan was 42 when GoldenEye launched his Bond era in 1995 
 Illustration: Quartz
 Pierce Brosnan was 42 when GoldenEye reached theaters in 1995, his first outing as James Bond. He played 007 in four films over seven years and was 49 when the last of them, Die Another Day, came out in 2002.
 Brosnan is Irish and was born in 1953. Timothy Dalton, who held the role immediately before him, was born in 1946. That puts seven years between the two men's births.
 The birth-year gap did not carry over to their debuts. Dalton was 41 when The Living Daylights opened in 1987. Brosnan was one year older when GoldenEye arrived.
 Dalton's run ended with Licence to Kill in 1989, when he was 43. Six years passed before GoldenEye came out. Brosnan started the job one year younger than Dalton was when he left it.
 Brosnan's films then came on a steady schedule. He was 44 in Tomorrow Never Dies in 1997 and 46 in The World Is Not Enough in 1999. The first three entries of his tenure arrived two years apart. Die Another Day followed after a three-year gap.
 Across those four films, Brosnan aged seven years on screen. His tenure outlasted Dalton's two films and Lazenby's single outing but fell short of the runs held by Moore and Craig.
 Brosnan's debut age made him the second-oldest of the official Bond actors at his start. Only Roger Moore began older, and Brosnan was three years younger than Moore at their respective debuts. Daniel Craig, who succeeded Brosnan, was four years younger in Casino Royale than Brosnan had been in GoldenEye.
 Brosnan's debut age was also five years past the age Ian Fleming's novel Moonraker gives the character.
 Brosnan had worked in the spy-thriller genre before taking the role. He appeared in The Fourth Protocol in 1987, eight years before GoldenEye and the same year Dalton made his Bond debut.
 In his final Bond film, Brosnan was eight years younger than Moore was in A View to a Kill.
 Daniel Craig was 38 in Casino Royale and held the role for 15 years 
 Illustration: Quartz
 Daniel Craig was 38 when Casino Royale opened in 2006. He went on to play James Bond for 15 years, the longest continuous stretch of any actor in the part.
 Craig was born in 1968, 15 years after Pierce Brosnan and 22 years after Timothy Dalton. His debut age put him below both of his immediate predecessors. Brosnan was 42 in GoldenEye, and Dalton was 41 in The Living Daylights. Craig arrived four years younger than Brosnan and three years younger than Dalton.
 That broke a pattern in the series. Roger Moore, Dalton and Brosnan had each started in the role at 41 or older. Only Sean Connery, in Dr. No, and George Lazenby, in On Her Majesty's Secret Service, debuted younger than Craig.
 His age climbed over the following films. He was 40 in Quantum of Solace, his second outing. He was 44 when Skyfall came out in 2012, still a year younger than Moore had been in Live and Let Die. He was 47 by the time of Spectre.
 At his fourth film, Craig was younger than two of his predecessors had been at the same point. Brosnan was 49 in Die Another Day, his fourth and last Bond film. That made him two years older than Craig in Spectre. Moore was 51 in the film Moonraker, his fourth outing, four years older than Craig at that stage. Connery was younger at the same point, at 35 in Thunderball.
 No Time to Die was Craig's fifth and final Bond film. He was in his early 50s across its long production and delayed release. The film opened in theaters in 2021, 15 years after Casino Royale.
 That span is the longest in the official series. Connery's six official films covered nine years. Brosnan's four ran from 1995 to 2002, a seven-year stretch. Dalton's films came out in 1987 and 1989. Craig's run lasted six years longer than Connery's and eight years longer than Brosnan's.
 Lashana Lynch was 33 as Nomi, the 007 agent in No Time to Die 
 Illustration: Quartz
 Lashana Lynch was 33 when No Time to Die reached theaters in 2021. She plays Nomi, an agent who carries the 007 number. She holds the code designation but does not play James Bond.
 Lynch was born on Nov. 27, 1987. When the film opened, she was about a month short of turning 34.
 Her character takes the number, not the name. That keeps her off the list of actors who have played Bond in the official Eon Productions films. Daniel Craig still plays Bond in No Time to Die, his final outing in the role. The film puts two holders of the 007 identity on screen together. One is the actor who has played Bond since Casino Royale. The other is the agent now assigned the number.
 Compared with the six Bond debuts, Lynch's age sits toward the younger end. She was older than George Lazenby and Sean Connery were when their first Bond films came out. Of all six debut ages, Connery's comes closest to hers. She was younger than the other four at their debuts.
 She was also younger than the age Ian Fleming's novel Moonraker gives Bond. Lazenby and Connery are the only Bond actors who debuted below that literary mark.
 The Bonds of the late 1980s and 1990s debuted well above her age. Timothy Dalton was 41 when The Living Daylights opened, eight years older than Lynch was in No Time to Die. Pierce Brosnan was 42 in GoldenEye, nine years older than Lynch at her 007 turn.
 The age gap with her co-star was wider still. Craig was born in 1968, 19 years before Lynch. He was in his early 50s across the film's long production and delayed release.
 The script also nods to her age. Bond calls Nomi "a disarming young woman" in No Time to Die. The remark comes from Craig's Bond, the character whose number she now holds.
